title: Winter and Visitor
premise: Jonah Galloway takes a teaching post in the snowbound town of Hollowmere, where a class of students vanished decades ago and the school quietly pretends otherwise. His photographs begin showing an extra chair—an empty seat that follows him from his grandmother's house to his classroom—and he learns the chair belonged to a child taken by the town's founding families in 1974 as payment for their prosperity. The 'visitor' is the collected memory of the taken children, seeking not vengeance but return: Jonah must recover what was stolen, even as the town's powerful elders, who feed on the borrowed years, try to make him the next offering. In the end Jonah gives back the ledger of names, dissolving the elders' power, though the frost claims him partially—he survives, but carries one of the children's memories forever, and the extra chair finally appears with someone sitting in it.
about_author: V. M. Nakamura is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing abandoned school records across the northern counties. They write horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the things that wait politely to be noticed.

chapters.title: The Position Is Still Open
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Jonah Galloway, arriving in Hollowmere by bus through freezing fog. The job posting had no closing date; the principal hires him before he finishes speaking. Emotional beat: uneasy relief—someone wanted him here too much.

chapters.title: Attendance Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He establishes his rituals: photographing documents, logging everything in a green notebook. Twenty-eight students enrolled; twenty-two attend. No one will say where the other six went. Beat: the comfort of routine curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Grandma's House Has One More Chair
chapters.summary: Jonah inherits and moves into his late grandmother's house at the edge of town. Developing an old roll of film, every photo—spanning forty years—shows an extra wooden chair against the wall. Beat: intimate violation; the past has been edited.

chapters.title: Six Empty Desks
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He finds the 1974 yearbook: six students' photos are scratched out. A custodian, Ruth Okafor, warns him that asking about them is how people 'get invited.' Beat: first ally, first threat.

chapters.title: What the Frost Writes
chapters.summary: POV shifts to eleven-year-old Wren, one of the missing, in a cold white elsewhere where a polite Visitor asks her to remember being forgotten. Beat: eerie tenderness—the horror is patient, almost kind.

chapters.title: The Founders' Portrait
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. In the school lobby hang portraits of five founding families. Under frost on the glass, new names appear overnight—his own among them. Beat: he is already on a list he never signed.

chapters.title: Documentation
chapters.summary: Jonah photographs the frost-names; in the developed prints the letters have rearranged into dates. All point to December 1974. Beat: his faith in records becomes terror when records start answering back.

chapters.title: Ruth Remembers Wrong
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. She recalls the winter of '74 vividly—but her memories contradict themselves each time she tells them, and her hands are colder than they should be. Beat: grief for a self that keeps being rewritten.

chapters.title: Parent-Teacher Night
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The parents of Hollowmere are uniformly warm, uniformly aged strangely well. When he mentions the six names, smiles don't drop—they sharpen. Beat: social horror; politeness as menace.

chapters.title: The Ledger in the Wall
chapters.summary: Following the chair's position in grandma's oldest photo, Jonah pries up floorboards and finds a ledger listing payments made to the town in 1974—each entry a child's name. Beat: revelation; the town was bought.

chapters.title: Chair Number Seven
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the white elsewhere, a seventh chair appears, facing hers. Something new is being prepared to sit in it. Beat: mounting dread aimed at Jonah without naming him.

chapters.title: The Aldermen Invite You
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A formal card invites him to dinner with the Aldermen, descendants of the founders. He goes, documenting secretly. The meal is lavish; no one eats. Beat: seduction of power—they offer him tenure, permanence, warmth.

chapters.title: Borrowed Years
chapters.summary: Alderman Corvus Hale's POV, the novel's first villain interiority. He explains nothing but thinks everything: the town's vitality is drawn from the taken children, and the supply is thinning. Beat: chilling banality of corruption.

chapters.title: Photographs Lie Now
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. His documentation turns traitor: photos show him smiling at things that aren't there, logs contain entries in his handwriting he never wrote. Beat: loss of his one reliable anchor.

chapters.title: Wren Finds the Window
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She discovers she can see through frosted glass into Jonah's classroom. She begins leaving messages in the frost patterns. Beat: hope kindling between two trapped people.

chapters.title: Frost on the Inside
chapters.summary: Jonah wakes to find frost on the inside of every window, spelling ATTENDANCE. Three more students are absent. Beat: escalation—the pattern is accelerating because he arrived.

chapters.title: The Missing-Class Problem
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. She finally tells Jonah the truth she's been made to forget nightly: she was the teacher in 1974. She let them take the six. Beat: confession, guilt, and the cost of survival.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The ledger's final page instructs: 'Returned in full, the account closes.' But the taken children aren't objects to hand back—they're held in the Aldermen's blood. Beat: understanding the true price of restitution.

chapters.title: Winter Break
chapters.summary: Jonah stays in Hollowmere over break; the town empties except for the Aldermen and the cold. The extra chair appears in his kitchen, closer each morning. Beat: isolation tightening like a fist.

chapters.title: Hale's Offer
chapters.summary: Corvus Hale visits Jonah's home, sits uninvited in the extra chair, and offers him immortality-by-proxy: sign the ledger as a founder, gain the borrowed years. Beat: temptation rendered intimately—power offered as belonging.

chapters.title: Found Family, Found Fault
chapters.summary: Jonah and Ruth form a fragile alliance over soup and evidence, joined by student Marisol Vega, whose brother is next on the attendance list. Beat: warmth as defiance—a found family forming inside the trap.

chapters.title: Marisol's Map
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. She's mapped every disappearance since 1974: they cluster around the old chapel under the reservoir. Beat: teenage courage outpacing adult caution.

chapters.title: Under the Ice
chapters.summary: Jonah, Ruth, and Marisol reach the drowned chapel's exposed foundations in a frozen-drawn-down reservoir. Inside: six small desks arranged around a chair. Beat: awe and horror fused; the site of the original theft.

chapters.title: The Ceremony of 1974
chapters.summary: Interlude in Wren's memory: the night the founders' children were traded, the adults singing carols while the Visitor counted heads. Beat: the novel's darkest chapter; complicity set to Christmas music.

chapters.title: They Know You Know
chapters.summary: Jonah returns to find his classroom ransacked, his notebook gone, Ruth hospitalized with 'exposure.' Beat: the cost arrives; allies are leverage now.

chapters.title: The Green Notebook Returns
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. His notebook reappears on his desk, its pages now recording future events—including tomorrow's date and the words JONAH SITS DOWN. Beat: fatalism versus free will.

chapters.title: Wren Speaks Through the Glass
chapters.summary: Wren reaches fully through the frost for one minute and tells Jonah the Visitor isn't the monster—it's a warden, keeping the children until the debt is honored. The Aldermen broke the contract's terms. Beat: reversal; the enemy is the living, not the dead.

chapters.title: Quorum
chapters.summary: Corvus Hale's POV. The Aldermen convene to vote on taking Jonah early, arguing like men discussing insurance. Two dissent. Beat: institutional evil deliberating procedurally.

chapters.title: The Dissenters
chapters.summary: Jonah meets the two dissenting Aldermen, elderly siblings who've kept their own secret ledger of guilt for fifty years. They offer testimony—if he can protect them until the solstice. Beat: fragile hope, ticking clock.

chapters.title: Exposure
chapters.summary: Ruth dies of cold in a heated hospital room, her last word a child's name. Jonah grieves and hardens. Beat: the midpoint's promise of found family pays its terrible price.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Jonah, Marisol, and the dissenters prepare to read the ledger aloud at the chapel as the contract requires. The frost writes patterns on every surface in town, converging toward the reservoir. Beat: gathering storm.

chapters.title: The Longest Night Begins
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs braided: the reading starts, the Aldermen arrive with police and neighbors, the crowd that benefits from the theft comes to stop the truth. Beat: confrontation of community complicity.

chapters.title: Attendance Taken
chapters.summary: The Visitor manifests at last—not monstrous but meticulous, calling the roll of 1974. Each name spoken thaws something; each Alderman ages visibly as borrowed years reclaim themselves. Beat: climax igniting; power literally draining.

chapters.title: Hale Refuses
chapters.summary: Corvus Hale seizes the ledger and burns it, declaring the debt void. The frost surges; the chapel begins to close like a mouth. Beat: climax crisis—destruction of the means of restitution.

chapters.title: Memory Is the Ledger
chapters.summary: Jonah realizes the burned pages survive where it matters: in Wren and the others, and in his own documented mind. He recites all six names from memory, adding Ruth's. Beat: theme crystallized—memory outlasts paper.

chapters.title: The Account Closes
chapters.summary: The Visitor accepts the recitation. The Aldermen collapse into ordinary old age; the town's unnatural warmth fails; real winter enters honestly for the first time in fifty years. Beat: catharsis through loss of false comfort.

chapters.title: Six Chairs, Occupied
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The white elsewhere opens; the children walk out through the thawing ice into dawn, choosing which memories to keep. Wren chooses to stay near Jonah. Beat: release, bittersweet and earned.

chapters.title: Spring Semester
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Weeks later: an investigation he'll never fully understand, a town learning to live unfrozen, Marisol's brother home. The extra chair remains in his kitchen—with a small girl sometimes sitting in it, doing homework. Beat: resolution; found family completed.

chapters.title: What Jonah Keeps
chapters.summary: Final chapter in Jonah's voice, journal-style. He still documents everything, but now some entries are letters to Wren, and some photographs include a seventh person smiling. Beat: peace with permanent change; memory as inheritance rather than wound.

chapters.title: Epilogue: The Next Posting
chapters.summary: Distant third person: a new teacher somewhere far away receives a job posting with no closing date, and a green notebook arrives in the mail with a note: 'Document everything. It helps.' Beat: cyclical chill softened into guardianship—the watcher tradition continues, benevolent this time.
